item.title: August 31, 2026 City Council
item.dc:creator: Sam Jacobson
item.description:
Location: Franklin Elks

Time: 6:00 PM

Agenda - No separate agenda provided as of 8/29/26. See page 2 of packet for agenda.

Packet

This is a standard City Council meeting, starting with public hearings, public comment, and then moving onto council business.

Below are my preliminary thoughts and initial positions going into the meeting. Please email me at sjacobson@franklinnh.gov if you would like to discuss further.

Agenda Items

1. Approval of Minutes

  • Summary:
    • Minutes from City Council Meetings in August.
      • August 3 is a regular city council meeting.
      • August 11 is a non-meeting as there was not a quorum.
      • August 14 is the approval of the FY27 budget.

How Sam Sees It:

  • No significant changes recommended.

2. Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) for Franklin Outing Club (FOC)

  • Summary:
    • In August the FOC brought their MOU forward and the City Council sent it back with revisions.
    • The changes to the draft MOU are as follows:
      • 50% premium cost sharing for city liability insurance.
      • Mutual notification if agreement is terminated.

How Sam Sees It:

  • I think this MOU writes down a lot of what has previously been happening between FOC and the City.
  • I think the City should pay for the premiums on the liability insurance policy. This places an unneeded burden on the FOC non-profit and is a departure from decades of precedent.
  • I am surprised to see the FOC taking on workers comp insurance as this was handled by the City in the past.
  • I am happy to see the first MOU come before the Council.
  • This set’s minimums on the City’s contribution to the FOC, but additional support or in kind support could be offered in the future on an ad hoc basis.

3. Public Hearing for Revenue from Sale of Surplus Fire and EMS Equipment

  • Summary:
    • Seeks to set a hearing at the next City Council meeting to accept ~$10,000 in revenue from equipment sales.

How Sam Sees It:

  • We should schedule and hold this hearing.

4. Emergency Plan Adoption

  • Summary:
    • The Fire chief, Police chief, and others developed emergency plans between May and July 2026.
    • Emergency plans reflect updates recommended by state agencies.
    • These plans help coordinate personnel and equipment in emergencies.
    • Plan was available for review by the public on May 7 and should be available on the City website.
    • The last time this plan was updated was in 2020.

How Sam Sees It:

  • I’m generally in favor of regularly updating emergency procedures.
  • The supplied link in the agenda does not work, I have not had a chance to review the plan.

5. FEMA floodplain Management

  • Summary:
    • The Federal Emergency Management Administration (FEMA) has added another requirement to flood insurance.
    • This is administrative and lack of action may cause loss of coverage.

How Sam Sees It:

  • I think we should approve this amendment so as not to lose insurance coverage, or reduce eligibility for residents.
  • It’s not clear to me what the amendment is, as the suggested language in the suggested motion is dated in the future (November 2026).

6. Parks and Recreation Fee Schedule

  • Summary:
    • Currently the fees associated for parks and recreation are listed and defined in the city code.
    • This seeks to move the fee schedule in the budget to connect it more closely to the budget process.
    • Moving out of the code allows more flexibility for the Parks and Recreation director and council to change rates as needed.

How Sam Sees It:

  • This motion came out of the parks and recreation committee.
  • I think we should move these fees out of the code and into the budget.

7. Electronic Use Policy

  • Summary:
    • The draft electronic device policy was kicked from the City Council to the Legislative committee on August 3rd.
    • The Legislative committee reviewed this policy on August 20, and added a handful of additional exceptions.
    • This policy is meant to:
      • Focus the council during meetings.
      • Prevent side discussions out of public view.
      • Set an expectation for use of different meeting aids.
    • These policies are not enforceable, but it is a commitment by the councilors.

How Sam Sees It:

  • I think we should adopt this as it enhances transparency and builds trust with the public.

8. Expand Definition of Park Asset

  • Summary
    • The Parks and Recreation department manages more than just Bessie Rowell Community Center (BRCC) but the code and policies governing the Parks and Recreation department are focused on BRCC.
    • This expands the definition of asset in the code to provide clearer legal foundation for things like permitting and use policies.

How Sam Sees It:

  • This came out of the Parks and Recreation committee
  • It’s mostly procedural and is a clarification that the director wanted for his policymaking.
  • These changes seems reasonable to me.

9. Public Hearings Revision

  • Summary:
    • This is a change that came out of legislative committee making three changes to public hearings:
      • Expands who can post public hearings to more than just the City Clerk.
        • This makes it easier for people like planning and zoning (who have their own legal requirements to notice hearings) to complete these obligations.
      • Shortens the required post time to seven days prior to the hearing from ten days prior to the hearing.
      • Removes requirement to post in the newspaper.

How Sam Sees It:

  • Note that removal of the newspaper does not mean public notice is not made; rather it recognizes that a newspaper may not be the best avenue for public hearing notices.
  • I’d like to see public hearings posted in cheaper more broadly accessible ways like email blasts, flashing signs on central street, website notifications.
  • These changes make sense to me and should be adopted.

10. Changes to Ordinance Revision Procedure

  • Summary:
    • This seeks to simplify and clarify the process for changing the city code.
    • The changes do things like:
      • Clarifies that public hearings are not mandatory for every ordinance change.
      • Removes the need to publish changes in the newspaper, and record in a physical book in City Hall.
      • Requires ordinance changes and new ordinances to come before the entire council.

How Sam Sees It:

  • I think these changes makes sense
  • It reduces the reporting needs, but maintains the public notice for changing ordinances.
  • It sets a more reasonable floor for ordinance changes; on a case by case basis the council could advertise ordinance changes more broadly.

11. Winnipasaukee River Basin (WRB) Transition

  • Summary:
    • The WRB manages wastewater throughout the lakes region, including Franklin.
    • The WRB is currently administered by NH department of Environmental services (NHDES)
    • The managers of the WRB suggest member communities manage the program themselves to save costs, instead of running through NH DES.
    • The WRB board has a couple of examples of poor management by NHDES wasting ratepayer dollars and notes that NH DES is focused on enforcement not operating.

How Sam Sees it:

  • I’m not ready to support this at this time.

Questions

  • How much do we pay into this system now, where is it trending for Franklin, and how much we can expect to pay under our own management.
  • Do we lose protection for Franklin’s cost and/or state support if we leave the NH DES management?

12. Set a September Workshop

  • Summary:
    • Set a workshop on September 14 on Robert’s rules.

How Sam See’s it:

  • I don’t think this is necessary.
  • I’d prefer it held the following Monday (9/21).

13. Proposed Charter Amendments - School Board

  • Summary:
    • Following public comment on the proposed amendment, the final amendment language has to be sent to the state for review.
    • See previous post for more information.

How Sam See’s it:

  • THis is a straightforward charter change with limited impact. It is a test on how to actually change the charter, while we have time to change it.
    • Changing the charter is like working a muscle, you have to start slow.

14. Proposed Charter Amendments - Neutralizing Gender Bias

  • Summary:
    • Following public comment on the proposed amendment, the final amendment language has to be sent to the state for review.
    • See previous post for more information.

How Sam See’s it:

  • This is a more consequential charter change that that impacts many different sections. It is a further test on how to actually change the charter.
    • Changing the charter is like working a muscle, you have to start slow.

Other Business

  • Appointing Deborah Burley to the Ward 1 Election Moderator.

item.title: August 20, 2026 Legislative
item.dc:creator: Sam Jacobson
item.description:
Location: Franklin Public Library

Date: August 20, 2026

Time: 6:00 PM

Agenda

Below is what we plan to discuss:

  1. Approve minutes from May 21 meeting and July 23
    • Minutes are located at the bottom right of the linked page.
  2. Charter amendment procedure
  3. Changes to public hearing procedure
  4. Ordinance procedure revisions
  5. Winter parking ordinance
  6. Curbside trash ordinance review
  7. Electronic device review
  8. Other business

Agenda Breakdown

1. Minute Approval

Brenda Demers drafted minutes from the May 21 and July 23 meeting, which I expect to approve with minimal changes. The committee was not prepared to review the May 21 minutes at our last meeting.

How Sam Sees it:

Brenda has historically done a fantastic job with the minutes. I don’t expect major changes.

2. Charter Amendment Procedure

Councilor Warner wants to develop a procedure for proposing Charter amendments. This is the beginning of that process.

How Sam Sees It:

I think the current process works fine - proposed changes come through legislative, then are brought to the full council. I don’t see a need for more formal procedure, but am open to additional discussion.

3. Changes to Public Hearing procedure

At the meeting on July 23, the City Manager brought forward this change to section 31 of the City code. This is intended to provide more flexibility for setting public hearings, 7 days rather than 10 days before a hearing, and remove the need to publish in the newspaper.

How Sam Sees It:

I think these changes are reasonable, 1 week of notice is pretty similar to 10 days of notice. Additionally, I think that the newspaper requirement is outdated as we do not have a newspaper that covers Franklin regularly or comprehensively. I could see replacing it with some kind of electronic (i.e. posting on the city website) instead.

4. Changes to Ordinance procedure

At the meeting on July 23, the City Manager brought forward this change to section 68 of the City code. There are a series of changes to this piece of the code, affecting how ordinances are amended:

  • All changes have to go before the full council
  • Public reading of the ordinance may be waived if there is a unanimous vote of the council
  • If needed an ordinance can be sent to legislative for additional reworking
    • The legislative committee presents its work at the next practicable council meeting
  • Removes the need for public hearings on standard ordinances
    • Pushes towards a public forum rather than a public hearing.

How Sam Sees It:

I like the flexibility this provides to legislative to respond when practicable as it gives more flexibility for a good faith effort of aligning schedules. I don’t like removing the public hearing requirement. The push to public forum vs public hearing is a semantic one that doesn’t really sit well with me. I understand that a public forum has fewer restrictions/noticing requirements, but the noticing is important. I don’t think every ordinance change needs to be listed in the newspaper, but I think the general public should be made aware of changes to the code and provided an opportunity to weigh in.

5. Winter Parking Ordinances

Director Chunn prepared a parking study; this committee will review and recommend ordinance changes. This study was not ready at the last meeting.

How Sam Sees It:

The time to start on parking is before the winter. I expect this to be multiple meetings, and involve significant discussion with the broader council.

The main issue I see is that the city says no one can park on streets overnight during a snow storm, but does not provide a place to park (section 248 of the city code). Looking at section 248, there are 3 sections (B, C, D) that all say the same thing - you are not allowed to park overnight on a street or parking lot unless signed. Violators would be towed. I think this could be consolidated into one section, and then make clear that the city will identify parking areas during snow storms that are valid. We need to know where there may be parking spots to direct people to before sending them there.

Additionally, folks need to be out of the parking lot soon after the snow storm so the lot could be cleared. This means violators would be towed. I think the city could identify one lot for this winter (i.e. off Winnipasaukee street) and see how it works (how many people use it etc. )

6. Curbside trash pickup ordinance

As part of the FY27 budget, the city manager proposed changes to the city trash collection. These require ordinance changes. These changes include:

  • Addition of fee language to the ordinances
  • Institution of a sticker based system
  • City still provides trash bins

How Sam Sees It:

These changes make sense and align with discussions the City Manager has had with the Council. This is the first step to implementing the fee system for pickup.

7. Electronic device policy review

During the August 3rd City Council meeting, the electronic device use policy was sent back to legislative for review. we were requested to add the following:

  • Exceptions for phone use for communications from family members

How Sam Sees It:

This is a reasonable exception to me. I’d also like to know which neighboring communities the City Manager spoke to when defining this policy.

8. Other Business

None at this time.

item.title: August 10, 2026 - Public Hearing on Charter Changes
item.dc:creator: Sam Jacobson
item.description:
Location: Franklin Public Library

Date: August 10, 2026

Time: 6:00 PM

Agenda

No packet has been provided for this hearing

This is a public hearing on two proposed changes to the Franklin city charter. It is a requirement of the charter amendment process described in RSA 49. The basic process is as follows:

  1. A charter amendment is proposed and passed by the City Council
    • The proposed amendments were crafted in the legislative committee in April and May and brought to the full Council on June 1.
  2. The proposed amendment is discussed in a public hearing.
    • The hearing scheduled for August 10th is that hearing.
    • If there are substantive changes, a new hearing is held.
  3. The proposed amendment is sent to the NH Secretary of State, Department of Revenue Administration and Attorney General for review.
    • They may require changes, which sends this back to step 1.
    • If approved, it goes to the city council for action.
  4. The Council votes to put it on the ballot (i.e. in an October election) for a vote from all registered voters.

Below are my preliminary thoughts and initial positions going into the meeting. Please email me at sjacobson@franklinnh.gov if you would like to discuss further. I am currently traveling for work, and likely will not be able to participate in this meeting fully.

If you would like to submit comment directly, you may do so via the city website.

Agenda Items

1. School Board Rename

Text of amendment

Summary:

  • The charter is inconsistent in how it refers to the elected body that oversees the schools. This replaces “board of education” with “school board”.

How Sam Sees It:

  • This is a simple, non-consequential change to the charter. I see this as a way to test how to actually change the charter. Franklin has not changed its charter voluntarily for years, perhaps decades.
  • This may help residents navigate the charter (i.e. easier searching for a colloquial phrase than a legal one from the 1960’s).

2. Neutralizing Gender Bias

Text of amendment

Summary:

  • Removes gendered language throughout the charter
    • For example the charter assumes that the city manager is a man or that the mayor is a man in certain provisions.

How Sam Sees It:

  • I see this as a more significant proposal. Women have led and will hopefully continue leading this community and our governing documents should recognize them.
  • While this does not substantively change city operation (we’ve had a woman serve as mayor under this biased charter), the bias in the charter is noticeable.
  • It provides further practice for making charter changes.

3. Discussion of the public hearing

Summary: - Following the public hearing the council needs to refer the proposed amendments (assuming there are no changes) to the clerk for filing with the state.

How Sam Sees It:

  • This is procedural, but important to react to public input.

item.title: August 03, 2026 City Council
item.dc:creator: Sam Jacobson
item.description:
Location: Franklin Elks

Time: 6:00 PM

Agenda

Packet

This is a standard City Council meeting, starting with public hearings, public comment, and then moving onto council business.

Below are my preliminary thoughts and initial positions going into the meeting. Please email me at sjacobson@franklinnh.gov if you would like to discuss further.

Note that this preview includes late items that have been distributed.

Agenda Items

1. Approval of Minutes

  • Summary:
    • Minutes from eight City Council workshops in June and July
      • Most of these are budget related.
    • Minutes from July 6th City Council meeting

How Sam Sees It:

  • No significant changes recommended.

2. Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) for Franklin Outing Club (FOC)

  • Summary:
    • In January, the City began requiring a signed memorandum of understanding (MOU) with outside entities, particularly non-profit organizations.
    • This is the first MOU to come before the council.
    • FOC has provided ski/snow recreation opportunities since 1963.
    • FOC operates and maintains all facilities and ski trails at the veterans memorial ski area.
    • FOC has to make an operating plan and approve it through the City.
    • MOU details
      • 21 year agreement
        • Can be terminated by 2/3 of City Council, or FOC with 90 day notice
      • Agreement evaluated annually
      • Possibility (i.e. required bookkeeping) of annual audit
      • FOC owns all concessions, expenses, utilities, machinery, equipment.
      • Changes to the lodge become the City’s
      • City pays for liability insurance, club pays for worker’s compensation insurance and liquor insurance.

How Sam Sees It:

  • I think this MOU writes down a lot of what has previously been happening between FOC and the City.
  • I am surprised to see the FOC taking on workers comp insurance as this was handled by the city in the past.
  • I do not like how much control this gives the city council over an independent entity; however they have reached mutual agreement on terms.
  • I am happy to see the first MOU come before the council.
  • This set’s minimums on the City’s contribution to the FOC, but additional support or in kind support could be offered in the future on an ad hoc basis.

3. Pump House Replacement

  • Summary:
    • FOC wants to demolish the pump house and replace with a larger pump.
    • This would allow better water transfer to snow making equipment.
    • FOC is working with NH Department of Environmental Services (DES) to authorize/evaluate water takings.
    • No cost to the city.
    • Permits provided to City Council.

How Sam Sees It:

  • This will save FOC volunteer time and enhance snow making.
  • This will not cost the city anything.
  • I think the council should approve this.

4. Lease Agreement for 117 Cheney Street

  • Summary:
    • Johnathan Wolfgram wants to lease a City owned vacant lot at the bottom of Cheney Hill for a personal garage.
    • Another neighbor does not want it used this way. -Lease details
      • Backdated to June 2026
      • 1 year lease
      • $155/month ($1,860/year)
      • 10% late fee if lease is not paid
      • Waive security deposit
      • Utilities, maintenance, snow, trash, paid by Mr. Wolfgram
      • Property improvements paid by Mr. wolfgram, to be approved by the city
      • Used as parking/storage
        • No hazardous waste storage
      • $1 million liability insurance held on the property and certificate provided to the City
      • City gets fire insurance, Mr. Wolfgram reimburses the city.
      • Sale of property terminates lease

How Sam Sees It:

  • This seems like a fair lease and a reasonable way to return property to the tax rolls.
  • A neighbor has come forward in the past to share impacts to neighborhood aesthetics for parking a truck there. This is as important as returning the property to use in my mind.
  • Other constituents have discussed the danger of backing out/parking on Cheney hill; this is similar to any resident living on Cheney Hill. Mr. Wolfgram and/or the drivers of the vehicles are responsible for handling their vehicles safely.
  • At this time, I’d approve this lease.

Questions

- Why is this lease backdated? 
- On what month would the city start collecting rent?

5. Electronic use policy for City Council and other meetings

  • Summary:
    • The council has requested a draft electronic use policy (phones, computers etc.)
    • All devices are subject to right to know (RSA 91-A) laws.
    • Policy
      • Applies to all members and any device (personal or otherwise) used during a meeting
      • Approved uses
        • Reviewing meeting material
        • Taking notes
        • Looking up factual information
        • Communicating with city staff
        • Participating in the meeting remotely
      • Prohibited uses
        • Personal texting/social media use
        • Inappropriate, disrespectful or unbecoming communication
        • Communication with another member of the body in private (i.e. texting another councilor how they’d vote privately)
        • Unauthorized recording
      • Devices should be silenced
      • No enforcement/penalties

How Sam Sees It:

  • I think the council should be able to use electronic devices.
  • I use a computer to take notes, organize meeting material, and communicate with constituents.
  • I have observed other councilors apparently texting each other during meetings which this may address
  • Without penalties, I am concerned this will not stop the texting at the table.
  • I would accept this policy as a start.

6. Moving debt and interest payments outside of the tax cap

  • Summary
    • At the July 29 public hearing the council postponed this motion
    • Moving $618,269 outside the tax cap and moving that money to the school budget
    • The motion was postponed for two reasons
      • Whether this was permissible under the city charter
        • We received a legal opinion from the city lawyer that this was permissible under the city charter
      • How much this would cost to a typical property owner
        • This would cost $0.53 per $1,000 of assessed value
        • For a $300,000 property it would be $159.00

How Sam Sees It:

  • I made this motion and think it should pass as the school is in need of funding from the city this year.
    • To date, this council has provided approximately $53,000
    • The total school budget is approximately $19,100,000
  • I am concerned as similar legally permissible methods have been voted down by this council with smaller dollar amounts.
  • I expect this to fail in favor of the third late item.

Late Item 1: Undoing previous council debt financing of ambulance

  • Summary
    • At the July 29 public hearing the council postponed this motion
    • In 2024 the council voted to order an ambulance and pay for it using debt
    • This council has voted to pay for it outside the tax cap.
    • This helps clarify the record/supersedes the older motion.

How Sam Sees It:

  • I am in favor of moving the ambulance outside the tax cap, this is one component of that.

Late Item 2: Purchase Ambulance outside of tax cap

  • Summary
    • At the July 29 public hearing the council postponed this motion
    • Cost of the ambulance is $466,289
    • Saves $100,000 in interest over the life of the loan
    • Cost is $0.40 per $1,000 of assessed property value
      • For a $300,000 property it would be $120.00

How Sam Sees It:

  • I’m generally in favor of moving the ambulance cost outside the tax cap.
  • I’m also sensitive to the stacked moves outside the tax cap (159 from moving debt outside for the school, and 120 for the ambulance).
  • This opens up budget for operational expense and is an appropriate use of Charter section C32-B.
  • I’d like to see the City budgeting and setting aside money for this and similar capital projects to lessen individual tax bills.
  • The $60,000 in savings is going to pay the Eversource litigation liability. This liability was paid in 2026 by this council taking money from the restricted fund balance. Taking money from the fund balance must be replaced, and this Council starts each year for the next 4 years, $60,000 behind.
    • Councilor Johnston worked to close the industrial park TIF, taking the ~$350,000 and moving it into the general roads account instead of using it to pay for the eversource liability. Money in the industrial park TIF was collected from the commercial properties in the industrial park. Effectively, the tax payers are paying for the Eversource litigation liability instead of commercial property owners. I think this is foolish.

Late Item 3: Authorizing the movement of debt outside the tax cap to pay for school

  • Summary
    • This is a repeat/formalized motion of the agenda item above.
    • Moving $618,269 outside the tax cap and moving that money to the school budget
    • We received a legal opinion from the city lawyer that this was permissible under the city charter
    • This would cost $0.53 per $1,000 of assessed value
      • For a $300,000 property it would be $159.00

How Sam Sees It:

  • I’m not sure why this is repeated, but I think we should move this money one time.

item.title: Pickups, Inflation, and Property Taxes
item.dc:creator: Sam Jacobson
item.description:
Tax relief for property owners comes from growing, not stagnation.

Franklin’s Tax Cap

Franklin is a community with a tax cap (technically it is a budget limitation). The tax cap is located in section C-32 of the City charter. It has multiple parts, however at it’s simplest level it restricts the amount of money the City can raise from property taxes in a given year. Each year, the City looks at how much it spent last year multiplies it by an estimate of inflation published by the US department of labor (Consumer Price Index Urban [CPIU]) and adds the value of new construction (“pickups”). This budget is used to pay for the services the city provides including:

  • Education
  • Police
  • Fire
  • Road Maintenance
  • Inspections
  • Registrations

Each budget listed on the City’s website includes a tax cap calculation page showing how the total tax to be collected is calculated. I tabulated that data for this approach.

This amount that the city of Franklin can collect in property taxes is shown graphically below. Note that Franklin budgets on a fiscal year that runs from July 1 to June 30, so fiscal year (FY) 2027 means the budget from July 1 2026 to June 30 2027. Note too that actual spent values in a given year will differ from this based on grants, debt, transfers, and other sources of revenue for the city.

Perhaps surprisingly, Franklin’s taxes keep growing, despite a tax cap in place. Overall, property taxes have grown from $10,081,532 in FY2006 to $20,997,771 in FY 27. This means over 21 years the Franklin budget has increased $10,916,239 or about $519,000/year. Most of that increase is due to inflation, some of that increase is due to growth in the City. As part of the budget, the finance office includes a budget cover sheet showing this calculation. This sheet is reviewed and approved by the New Hampshire department of revenue (DRA).

Consumer Price Index - Urban

The CPIU is the consumer price index - urban and calculates the percentage change in the cost of goods year to year (i.e. inflation). It is set at the federal level and includes things like the changes in milk and eggs. It does not include things like the cost of health insurance or the cost of pension obligations. The CPI-U is developed as an individual or family’s index of inflation, thus it is not really appropriate for a city with employees like Franklin. Nonetheless, the charter defines and demands the use of the CPIU as the maximum increase of tax year to year.

Pickups

Pickups are new construction that occurred over the course of the year. Imagine a new building that is built on a vacant lot; this is a new addition to the tax rolls and therefore represents growth in the city. That new property is taxed, and the value of those taxes are pickups. Pickups can also include improvements rather than a whole new building.

This chart shows how much money is added to the total allowable tax to be collected by from inflation/CPIU (red) and pickups (blue). Every year, the budget increases; either due to inflation (red) or new construction (blue). Times when inflation is extremely low (FY2010, 2009-2010) or extremely high (FY21, 2020-2021) represent macro economic forces acting on Franklin (2008 housing crash and covid-19 respectively). Typically the CPIU increases the city budget by ~$300,000.

Pickups are more variable, typically lower than the CPIU and more within Franklin’s control. While they track macroeconomic trends, in some cases they defy them. Franklin increases pickups when individuals and/or businesses choose to move to Franklin or when residents improve their homes. Budgets where pickups exceed the CPIU suggest growth in excess of inflation is occurring. This can provide real tax relief for property taxpayers in Franklin and/or maintain services.

A final way to look at this is as a percentage of the overall budget - how much are each of these revenue increase items impacting the overall city’s ability to spend?

This chart shows the dollar amounts divided by the total allowable taxes to be raised. Franklin’s budget is growing every year, and that most of that growth comes from inflation adjustment, not real growth. From FY17 to FY19 sustained growth occurred, however since then, Franklin has been relying on inflation indices to fund its operation. The CPIU does not account for all of the costs of running a city (e.g. health insurance). This chart shows that Franklin residents are paying more and getting less. Instead of capping taxes, the Franklin tax cap is capping services. We are paying more and getting less.

item.title: July 29, 2026 - Public Hearing on FY27 Budget
item.dc:creator: Sam Jacobson
item.description:
Location: Franklin Elks Lodge

Date: July 29, 2026

Time: 6:00 PM

Agenda

Packet

This is a public hearing on the Fiscal Year 2027 (FY27) budget.

Below are my preliminary thoughts and initial positions going into the meeting. Please email me at sjacobson@franklinnh.gov if you would like to discuss further.

If you would like to submit comment directly, you may do so via the city website.

Check out the Budget hub for department specific run-downs.

Agenda Items

1. FY27 Budget Summary

Summary:

  • Likely this is a discussion/response to the public hearing.

How Sam Sees It:

This is a precursor to resolution 2-27 below.

2. Resolution 02-27: Approving the FY 27 Budget

Summary:

  • Approves the budget as discussed over the months of June and July.
  • Major changes include:
    • Underfunding the School Board approved budget by $2.2 million dollars.
      • Cuts sports
      • Cuts a middle school nurse
      • Cuts a kindergarten teacher
      • Cuts a custodian
      • Cuts maintenance budget at each school
      • See budget hub for more details.
    • Creation of sticker program for curbside trash pickup.
      • On average, $100 for each trash can for curbside pick up.
    • 7% increase in water rate.
    • $40,000 decrease in legal funding.
    • Special ~$100 assessment for ambulance (see below).
    • Reductions in personal protective equipment and certifications in Municipal services.

How Sam Sees It:

I think this budget does not adequately fund the school district. I’ve tried repeatedly without success to shift money from obvious sources (City Manager’s contingency fund) and less obvious sources (open police positions) within the city budget to help the school. The majority of this Council is not willing to provide for the children in the public schools.

3. Resolution 03-27: Direct Spending for the ambulance

Summary:

  • Authorizes $466,289 to buy an ambulance.
  • Utilizes city charter (section 32-B) to pay capital expenses outside of tax cap.
  • Opens ~$60,000 for the next 5 years in budget space under the tax cap for operational expenses.
  • Estimated cost for a taxpayer is $0.37 per mill of assessed home value.
    • On a $300,000 house, this is should be $111 on the december tax bill.

How Sam Sees It:

  • This saves money on interest payments in the longer term.
  • This opens up budget for operational expense and is an appropriate use of Charter section C32-B.
  • I’d like to see the City budgeting and setting aside money for this and similar capital projects to lessen individual tax bills.
  • The $60,000 in savings is going to pay the Eversource litigation liability. This liability was paid in 2026 by this council taking money from the restricted fund balance. Taking money from the fund balance must be replaced, and this Council starts each year for the next 4 years, $60,000 behind.
    • Councilor Johnston worked to close the industrial park TIF, taking the ~$350,000 and moving it into the general roads account instead of using it to pay for the eversource liability. Money in the industrial park TIF was collected from the commercial properties in the industrial park. Effectively, the tax payers are paying for the Eversource litigation liability instead of commercial property owners. I think this is foolish.

4. Resolution 02-27: Override previous council action to buy ambulance

Summary:

  • In 2024, the City Council voted to buy the ambulance using debt.
  • Payments are not required until the ambulance is received (i.e. in 2027).
  • This City Council voted in 2026 to buy the ambulance outright.
  • This motion clarifies the history of the motions shifting form debt to outright purchase.

How Sam Sees It:

  • This is a housekeeping motion following the current council’s desires.

item.title: July 27, 2026 - Public Hearing on Trestle Bridge
item.dc:creator: Sam Jacobson
item.description:
Location: Franklin Elks Lodge

Date: July 27, 2026

Time: 6:00 PM

Agenda

Packet

This is a public hearing on the trestle bridge project.

Below are my preliminary thoughts and initial positions going into the meeting. Please email me at sjacobson@franklinnh.gov if you would like to discuss further.

If you would like to submit comment directly, you may do so via the city website

Agenda Items

1. Trestle Bridge Project

Summary: - The city of Franklin has an 80/20 match from the state to address the structural issues on the trestle bridge and turn it into a walkable structure. This means if the city pays 1 Million dollars, the state pays 4 Million dollars. - If the city pays 0 dollars, the state pays 0 dollars. - In the past, the city council voted to accept this grant and replace the trestle. The engineers proposed the following options: 1. Rebuild using existing timbers and foundations as much as possible. 2. Rebuild using all new timbers and new foundations following the same bridge design. 3. Rebuild using engineered wood product (“glulam”) following the same bridge design. 4. Rebuild using steel following a modern bridge design. 5. Demolish the trestle. - Each option costs about 1 million dollars to the city. - Using more modern methods (e.g. concrete foundations) is easier to contract out and more certain to estimate costs. - Maintenance costs generally go down as the materials become more engineered (wood costs more to maintain than glulam which costs more than steel)

How Sam Sees It:

I’m most in favor of option 2 above - rebuilding using timbers and modern methods for foundations. I think this retains the character of the bride, while being keeping costs reasonable. Critically, the current timbers are decaying, so reuse feels like a lot of work with little payout. Using modern methods (e.g. concrete foundations) is likely more stable and easier to contract out, likely reducing costs.

Maintenance costs may be higher, but I think this retains the character of the bridge for decades to come. Not acting on this grant will almost certainly make it more difficult to win grants from this state agency in the future. This project will hit the FY28 budget (not this year) so the council has time to raise/think about where to find the money to pay for this.

item.dc:creator: Sam Jacobson

This is the seventh meeting of the budget review process in the City. This will be a workshop meeting.

Agenda Items

1. Budget Discussion

Throughout the month of June, the City Council reviewed the City Manager’s proposed budget line-by-line. This is a chance for the City Council to see where the City Manager wants to spend money.

How Sam Sees It

At the meeting on 7/7, there were two main budget moves: 1. Councilor Warner cobbled 15k from MSD road maintenance lines to fund an assessment study focused on valuing commercial property. 2. Moves by Councilor Carrier and myself to try to get more money to the school. Below is a shortlist of what we attempted. The draft minutes provide a complete record of motions and votes.

  1. Fund services outside the tax cap
  • Reason: This retains levels of service for the city departments, however residents would have to fund the school. Note the tax cap remains in place under these methods as the council cannot unilaterally break the tax cap.
    • Method 1: Funding for required services (special ed) (using Section 32A of the City Charter)
    • Method 2: Funding for reduced state grant revenue (downshifting). This is the 2% revenue line change in section 32A of the charter.
  1. Shifting money underneath the tax cap
  • Reason: This reduces city services and/or increases liability for the city but reduces tax burden on residents.
    • Method 1: Directly change the budgetary split between city and school
    • Method 2: Reduce money from the City Manager’s contingency budget
    • Method 3: Reduce money for open positions (police)
    • Method 4: Reduce, not eliminate, new contracted service in city manager’s office (payroll, trust services)

Councilor Carrier and I made repeated motions to move different amounts of money using the above methods. The council cannot fund individual line items; we must fund a bottom line budget number for the school. The school board directs how that money is spent. Nevertheless we tried the following:

  • $2.25 million to meet the school board approved budget; or
  • $1 million dollars to offset some of the special ed costs; or
  • $278,000 to fund athletics; or
  • $58,000 for adult education.

All of this was rejected by the broader council.

I am stuck. The majority of this council has rejected using any method to move any amount of money to the school. At the same time, this council has not affirmed a final budget number for the school. As presented by the school board, funding at the traditional budget amount eliminates more than 16 positions, arts, athletics and potentially increases liability for the city.

item.title: July 6, 2026 City Council
item.dc:creator: Sam Jacobson
item.description:
Location: Franklin Elks

Time: 6:00 PM

Agenda

Packet

This is a standard City Council meeting, starting with public hearings, public comment, and then moving onto council business.

Below are my preliminary thoughts and initial positions going into the meeting. Please email me at sjacobson@franklinnh.gov if you would like to discuss further.

Agenda Items

1. Amending Non-public meeting minutes

  • Summary:
    • The council entered non-public on May 19 but did not follow proper procedure to seal the minutes of the non-public meeting.
    • The purpose of the non-public session was not stated.
    • Motions to seal and return were not made as roll-call vote.
    • These issues can be rectified after the fact.

How Sam Sees It:

  • These are relatively minor procedural issues, though they should be corrected.

2. Approval of Minutes

  • Summary:
    • Minutes from the various budget workshops in June, City council meetings in June, and non-public meetings in May.
    • 10 separate minutes to approve.

How Sam Sees It:

  • These are a lot of minutes.
  • It will be hard to review all of these in time for the meeting monday.
  • I’d like to approve the minutes.
  • To date, minutes have typically had minor clerical issues.

3. 2023 Tax Lien properties

  • Summary:
    • Owners of 35 properties have not paid their property taxes since 4/11/2024
      • 1 land
      • 10 land and building
      • 23 Mobile homes in park
      • 1 mobile home park land
    • link to list of lien properties
    • The tax collector typically works with th owners in hardship
    • Total outstanding balance is ~$63,000 ranging from $400-$9,000 on individual properties

How Sam Sees It:

  • Tax deeding property is not the first action of the city.
  • Tax deeding a property typically means removing it from the rolls, which represents lost revenue for the city.
  • Property owners have to pay their taxes to support city functions that they get the benefits of.
  • The city should deed these properties and work to get them to paying owners.

Questions

  • Is this a typical number of tax deed properties?

4. Authorize Fire engine purchase (split between two years)

  • Summary
    • The fire department (FD) is budgeting for a new engine to replace one of two active engines in the city.
    • The full price is ~$1.1M and the FD proposes to buy it in sections; ~$550,000 in Fiscal year (FY) 2028 and ~$550,000 in Fiscal year (FY) 2029.
    • The engine set to be replaced is difficult to service and was out of operation for maintenance reasons for more than 50 days this year.

How Sam Sees It:

  • I appreciate the FD budgeting this across two years and I’d like to hear if they have any revenue streams to cover it.
  • This is the prime application of a capital improvement exemption from the tax cap. I’d consider voting to exempt the cost from the tax cap calculation in 2028.
  • Since we can plan for this cost, we should budget for it.

5. Update Wetlands Ordinance

  • Summary
    • City of Franklin (75 ft setback) is more protective than the state (50 ft setback) regarding septic systems near wetlands.
    • The proposed revision allows septic systems 25 feet closer to wetlands than now.

How Sam Sees It:

  • I think we can change our statute to match the state, providing we highlight that in other cases (e.g. surface water bodies) the largest setback (75 ft) still applies.
    • For instance, installing a septic system near webster lake still needs a 75 ft setback, even if this change is accepted.
  • I think section 300-8 suggests that the more stringent rule applies (i.e. Franklin’s rule would apply)

6. Stiffen penalties for junkyards

  • Summary
    • Currently the city can charge up to $100/day for code violations.
    • The state allows up to $550/day for code violations.
    • The suggested change would link city penalties to the relevant state code and make fines for code violations larger.

How Sam Sees It:

  • I think this makes sense, especially in the extreme cases of years of non-compliance (evidenced by 528 Prospect street).
  • There is still discretion in the ordinance based on the severity of the fine.

7. Land sale on East Bow Street

  • Summary
    • The owner of 102 East Bow Street has made an offer of $3,000 for 0.13 acres of vacant city land abutting their property.
    • This property generated ~$600 in taxes last year that could be returned to the rolls; however merging properties is not necessarily additive. More or less than that might be captured from the new value of the property.
    • Abutters have been notified as of the previous (June 1) city council meeting; no additional bids have been received.

How Sam Sees It:

  • $3,000 still seems low
  • I’d like to hear if the City Manager has engaged in any negotiations with the bidder.

8. Amateur radio club lease

  • Summary
    • The city leases a radio repeater antenna to the amateur radio club
    • The city has leased this property since 1987
    • Proposed (continuation) lease is
      • $1/year
      • 5 years term
      • Limited use without additional city input
      • Club responsible for upkeep and utilities
      • City indemnified and club must retain insurance

How Sam Sees It:

  • This appears to be a well written lease, with reasonable terms
  • The $1 annual payment seems low, and I’d like to know why it is so low.

8. Other business

  • Council appointments
  • Ward 1 election moderator
    • Only one applicant.

Late items

Council to put a charter commission on October 2026 Ballot

  • Summary:
    • A charter commission is a group that rewrites the Franklin city charter
    • This is in contrast to making amendments/additions piecemeal
    • The charter commission process is essentially as follows (outlined in RSA 49):
      1. Charter commission is voted on a ballot
      2. Members of the charter commission develop a draft charter to place on the ballot the following year.
      3. The new charter, if approved, takes place the following year.

How Sam Sees It:

  • I think it is too late to put the charter commission question on the October 2026 ballot.
  • I’m in favor of a belt and suspenders approach; let’s develop a charter commission and submit edits to the charter as possible/practicable.
  • If the commission vote fails, e’ll still have needed edits to the charter.
